title: Mutually Assured AI Malfunction [Dan Hendrycks]
summary: Dan Hendrycks argues that a US race to superintelligence would provoke Chinese sabotage, and proposes deterrence by mutual AI sabotage, chip non-proliferation and competitiveness instead.

assertions.quote: They will either want to prevent such projects or they want to steal um it and so that looks like sabotage for instance for prevention.

verdicts.note: The logic mirrors preventive strikes on nuclear programmes, but no state has yet attacked a rival's AI project and the claim rests on untested strategic reasoning.

SIPRI says technological imbalance can make a weaker nuclear state doubt its second strike and tempt it to strike first, which fits the mechanism for AI-enabled counterforce rather than decisive AI superiority in general.

RAND argues that a state that sees AI tracking forces near its launchers could believe it must 'use it or lose it', a cycle of distrust that could incite a conflict neither side intended; the scenario is counterforce, not general AI dominance.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue rivals will not accept a large AI disadvantage and would sabotage a threatening project, escalating from espionage and cyberattacks to possible kinetic strikes on datacenters; a policy argument, not evidence that such attacks will happen.

assertions.quote: One is this would be extremely escalatory.

verdicts.note: Analysts widely flag the AI race as a source of tension, but it has so far stayed economic and technological, and forecasters see no near-term war driven by it.

RAND says Russia and China believe the US is using AI to threaten their nuclear forces' survivability, mutual distrust that 'could prove catastrophic in a crisis'; it is about counterforce fears, not a race for AI supremacy as such.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue that a US superintelligence Manhattan Project would alarm China, invite preemptive attack and escalate tensions rather than secure stability; argued scenarios, low confidence as prediction.

assertions.quote: this could lead to some type of deterrence dynamic

verdicts.note: Mutual assured AI malfunction is a proposed strategy with no historical test; whether AI projects are detectable and sabotageable enough for it to work is unknown.

This is the paper's central MAIM thesis: because a rival's AI project is easy to sabotage, states must expect any bid for monopoly to be maimed, giving deterrence without treaties; an untested proposal by its advocates.

assertions.quote: for analyzing this in a geopolitical way, it's useful to model this as nuclear cam and bio.

verdicts.note: AI shares dual-use and proliferation features with nuclear technology, but it is diffuse, commercially driven and has no single destructive threshold like a bomb.

RAND workshop participants agreed the legal structures and norms used against nuclear proliferation cannot be copied for military AI because the two technologies are too different, which limits the analogy.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue that the closest analogy for AI is nuclear and other dual-use technology, comparing today's 'AI Manhattan Projects' to the bomb; this is an argued analogy, not a measured resemblance.

CNAS argues AI is a general-purpose technology like computers or the combustion engine, not a discrete weapon like missiles, and that militaries' pursuit of it looked like routine adoption rather than a fervent arms race (as of 2021).

assertions.quote: I think compared to nuclear weapons, I think it's harder to make cutting edge GPUs given a billion dollars.

verdicts.note: Leading-edge chipmaking depends on a few firms and tools no state replicates alone, while several poor states have built bombs, though the cost comparison is rough.

assertions.quote: non-prololiferation in this case of of AI chips to rogue actors like North Korea or Iran or adversaries um uh through export controls

verdicts.note: Controls raise costs and slow access, but chip smuggling and cloud access have repeatedly leaked advanced chips to restricted buyers.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang propose compute security (tracking chips, stopping smuggling, geolocation features) to keep chips from rogue actors, a nonproliferation plan whose effectiveness they argue for but do not show.

assertions.quote: We want secure supply chains so that if Taiwan is invaded, our AI chips aren't cut off.

verdicts.note: Taiwan makes the large majority of the most advanced logic chips, and new US fabs cover only a small share of that capacity so far.
ODNI judges that a China-Taiwan conflict may disrupt US access to semiconductor technology and tech supply chains, a disruption rather than the full cut-off the claim states.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang call dependence on Taiwan for advanced AI chips a critical vulnerability and say a blockade or invasion 'may spell the end of the West's advantage in AI'; an assessment, not a supply analysis.

assertions.quote: software on critical infrastructure for various forms of critical infrastructure is more of a sitting duck

verdicts.note: CFR's 2026 expert survey rates a highly disruptive AI-enabled cyberattack on US critical infrastructure as moderate likelihood and high impact, a plausible serious risk rather than evidence it would cripple a country, and not tied to wartime.

SIPRI says AI can multiply cyber operations against nuclear command systems and that US-China dialogue flags cyberattacks on dual-use systems, which supports the mechanism but not crippling of national infrastructure.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang name an AI-enabled cyberweapon that could suddenly and comprehensively destroy a state's critical infrastructure as a possible 'subnuclear superweapon'; an argued possibility with no demonstrated case.

assertions.quote: there's a very strong incentive to for instance make the drones more autonomous um uh because they can be jammed.

verdicts.note: In Ukraine heavy jamming has driven both sides toward terminal autonomy and fibre-optic drones.

assertions.quote: that's potentially sufficient for a global catastrophe

verdicts.note: In the 2022 XPT tournament the median forecast that AI kills more than 10% of humanity within five years by 2100 was 2.13% for superforecasters and 12% for AI domain experts, so both groups treat an AI catastrophe this century as a real possibility, though superforecasters put it at a low probability.

In the WEF's survey of over 1,300 experts, Adverse outcomes of AI is the risk that rises most in the rankings, from #30 over two years to #5 over ten years (a global risk being one that would hit a significant share of global GDP or population), so experts see AI as a serious global risk, but this is a severity ranking based on perceptions, not a probability that AI causes a catastrophe.

RAND's experts set aside the 'Hollywood nightmare' of malevolent AI but feared more reliance on AI could cause new catastrophic mistakes in nuclear decisions; most AI experts did not see superintelligence as imminent or inevitable.

In a survey of 2,778 published AI researchers, those asked about AI causing human extinction or severe disempowerment within 100 years gave a median 5% and mean 14.4% (n=655), and a majority gave at least 5% across questions; expert opinion with framing effects and a 15% response rate, not a forecast record.

WEF's risk survey ranks adverse outcomes of AI technologies #5 of 33 risks over ten years (up from #30 over two), a perception of severity among surveyed leaders rather than evidence of a coming catastrophe.

In the 2022 XPT tournament the median superforecaster put the risk of an AI-caused catastrophe (over 10% of humans dead) by 2100 at 2.13% and the median AI expert at 12%: both groups see it as possible, at low to moderate odds.

assertions.quote: So I I think loss control risks from recursion are um uh very high um and shouldn't be pursued.

verdicts.note: No fully automated AI research loop exists yet, so the size of the control risk cannot be measured.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue that with today's safeguards a full-throttle intelligence recursion (AI automating AI research) would make losing control 'highly likely and the default'; an argument, not evidence.

WEF says the more AI agents are used in R&D to develop AI, the greater the risk their developers cease to understand how the systems work, and the harder governance becomes; it names a risk without calling it high.

assertions.quote: due to competitive pressures AI is it gets more intertwined in the economy

verdicts.note: Firms and militaries are adopting AI for competitive reasons, but how far decision authority will be handed over is still uncertain.

RAND expects AI to be given more prominence in road-to-war, escalation and even launch decisions, almost certainly, as firms and governments rush to use it; the evidence is military, not society-wide.

SIPRI says the pursuit of strategic advantage, especially acting at machine speed, may push nuclear-armed states to deepen AI integration despite human-control principles; this covers the military domain only.

CNAS argues competitive pressure could drive militaries to speed up operations and remove humans from the loop even if they would rather not; that supports the mechanism for militaries, not for societies at large.

WEF says incremental AI improvements could produce a creeping, structural shift of power from humans to AI over the next decade as agents take over human functions; a scenario, not a forecast with odds.

XPT forecasters split on whether humans would hand advanced AI control over critical systems: lower-risk forecasts said we might not, or would regulate, higher-risk forecasts said AI would likely be given control.
